{{nihongo|'''Awaga Jinja'''|粟鹿神社|qq=}} is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|qid=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine}} in the Santocho Awaga neighborhood of the city of {{ill|Asago, Hyōgo|en|Asago, Hyōgo|qid=Q720402|lt=Asago}} in {{ill|Hyōgo Prefecture|en|Hyōgo Prefecture|qid=Q130290|lt=Hyōgo Prefecture}}, {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|qid=Q17|lt=Japan}}. It is one of the two shrines (along with [[Izushi Shrine|Izushi Jinja]]) which claim the title of ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of former {{ill|Tajima Province|en|Tajima Province|qid=Q1053727|lt=Tajima Province}}. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on October 17.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese|qq=}}</ref>
==Enshrined ''kami''==
The main ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Awaga Jinja are:
* {{nihongo|'''Amenomisari'''|天美佐利命||qq=}}
* {{nihongo|'''Hiko imasu no Ōkimi'''|日子坐王命||qq=}}, the third prince of the 9th {{ill|Emperor Kaika|en|Emperor Kaika|qid=Q333548|lt=Emperor Kaika}} and the great-grandfather of the 12th {{ill|Emperor Keikō|en|Emperor Keikō|qid=Q329723|lt=Emperor Keikō}}.
* {{nihongo|'''[[Hoori|Hoori]]'''|日子穂穂手見尊||qq=}}, third son of [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto|Ninigi]] and [[Konohanasakuya-hime]]; grandfather of {{ill|Emperor Jimmu|en|Emperor Jimmu|qid=Q200188|lt=Emperor Jimmu}}.
==History==
The origins of Awaga Jinja are unknown. According to the shrine's legend, it was founded during the reign of the legendary {{ill|Emperor Suinin|en|Emperor Suinin|qid=Q314850|lt=Emperor Suinin}}. A local noble, Ohiko Hayami offered to the Imperial Court to build a shrine to worship the Amenomisari, as this ''kami'' was an [[Mitama#Ara-mitama and nigi-mitama|''arashin'']] (rough deity) which needed placating. His great-grandson took the surname "Kambe" and was the ''[[kuni no miyatsuko]]'' of Tajima.  The shrine first appears in the historical documents in tax records for Tajima Province dated 737. It appears thereafter in the various historical chronicles in the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|qid=Q193292|lt=Heian period}}, including the ''[[Engishiki]]'' and the ''[[Wamyō Ruijushō]]''. The ''Engishiki'' lists it as a {{nihongo|''Myōjin Taisha''|名神大社|||qq=}}. During the {{ill|Sengoku period|en|Sengoku period|qid=Q204023|lt=Sengoku period}},  {{ill|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|en|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|qid=Q187550|lt=Toyotomi Hideyoshi}} occupied the area in 1580, he confiscated the territory of the shrine, which fell into decline. Under then [[:en:Edo Period|Edo Period]] [[Tokugawa shogunate]], the area became {{ill|Izushi Domain|en|Izushi Domain|qid=Q10863249|lt=Izushi Domain}}, ruled by the [[Koide clan]] followed by the {{ill|Sengoku clan|en|Sengoku clan|qid=Q11378184|lt=Sengoku clan}}.<ref name="Yoshiki">{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese|qq=}}</ref>
During the {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|qid=Q3125096|lt=Meiji era}} era of {{ill|State Shinto|en|State Shinto|qid=Q1197248|lt=State Shinto}}, the shrine was rated as a village shrine in 1872 and promoted to a prefectural shrine in 1879 under the [[Modern system of Ranked Shinto Shrines]].<ref>Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 125.</ref><ref name="Okada">{{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese|qq=}}</ref>
The [[Honden]] was built in 1880 in the ''[[Nagare-zukuri]]'' style and is a three by two bay building. The [[Haiden (Shinto)|Haiden]] is a four by three bay building. There is a small hill behind the main shrine which has what appears to be the remnants of a moat. The shrine refers to this as the "tomb of the god", but it is not certain if this is an ancient ''[[kofun]]'' or not, as it has never been excavation. However, from 1999 to 2004, an [[archaeological excavation]] was conducted in the vicinity of the precincts due to the construction of the Kitakinki Toyooka Expressway, and the foundations of structures and a medieval stone paved approach have been found, indicating that the shrine was once much larger than it is at present.
The shrine is located about 30-minutes on foot from {{ill|Yanase Station|en|Yanase Station|qid=Q870907|lt=Yanase Station}} on the {{ill|West Japan Railway Company|en|West Japan Railway Company|qid=Q502125|lt=West Japan Railway Company}} [[:en:Sanin Main Line|Sanin Main Line]].
